I strongly recommend you do not buy this iPod.I bought it to replace my much loved 3G Nano, recently lost at Boston Logan.  At first, the 6G Nano appealed because of it's cool appearance and compact size.  But actual use quickly proved this is an inferior product well below Apple's usual high standards.1)  The battery life is abysmal.  I could never get over 10 hours of play time, and that's at half volume and barely using the screen.  Apple advertises 24 hours.  Do a web search and you'll find many people with this complaint.2)  Ergonomically, this thing is a disaster.  Where to begin?...- The multitouch screen has no place on a device this small and intended for sports.  It's touchy, and requires considerable attention to operate because of its tiny size, and usually needs two hands to use (one to hold the unit and the other to work the screen).  Though Apple portrays it as ideal for sports, the need to focus on the screen and use two hands makes it supremely inconvenient when you are doing most athletic activities.  In contrast, the click-wheel Nanos could easily be worked one handed.- By its very nature, the touch screen requires more taps and gestures to achieve the same result as the click-wheel.- The screen is not bright enough to be used in sunlight, again conflicting with its advertising as being great for use during sports.- The shape, even down to the clip, is so symmetrical, it is not easy to determine the orientation just by feel.  This makes using the clip problematic because it is easy to press on one side of it thinking that that's the opening side, when, in fact, it's not.  Again, no touch annunciation.- The tiny screen makes large playlists slow to navigate, and forces your attention to the screen while you do so.  Once more, the design of the Nano does not make it easy to use it while doing something else (like running).3)  Others have pointed out that the feature set has been reduced compared to 5G, while the price has not.  I'd consider it a fair trade if the design really lived up to its billing, and was functional and ergonomically friendly.  As it is not, the value of this Nano is exceptionally poor.The real disappointment is that the many failings of this device are mostly due to bad engineering and design, which is very unlike Apple.  It also strikes me as having been the result of a focused effort to cut the cost of production of the Nano to an all-time low while somehow justifying keeping the retail price the same.  In other words, corners were cut, polish was applied, and the result is a truly bad product.Another reviewer made a fantastic point when he calculated that the Amazon one-star ratings for the previous generation of Nano was only about 1% of the total ratings received, whereas one-star ratings for the 6G is over 20% of its total reviews.Case closed.  The Nano 6G went back to the Apple Store tonight for a refund.******************************Edit:  I bought a refurbished Nano 5G from the Apple Store.  The difference between this and the 6G I returned is night and day.  The 5G is so much easier to control, the larger shape is natural and comfortable in the hand yet still small enough to be unobtrusive, the screen is brighter, the battery life is substantially better - in short, this is a superior product in all respects except for the lack of a clip.I stand firmly on my original review:  the 6G Nano is by far the worst iPod Apple has ever made.
summary: The only Apple product I've ever returned for a refund

Many of the shots had to be taken by guesswork which was totally frustrating and the results were even more disappointing because I simply could not zoom in or out properly to frame the shot. The majority of the photos missed most of her body and others were not centred or zoomed in too much or too little.I will be checking to see if one of the camera's modes allows for better night time illumination, but it shouldn't have to be so difficult to find if it is there at all.Bottom LineGreat camera for good lighting conditions but forget it if you want to do portraits in darkness. Panasonic's engineers should try out some Canon cameras for night time performance to see what the competition is offering. Because of this flaw I will have to look for another camera with good overall performance. You can rest assured that it won't be a Panasonic this time.

Update: June 5th 2014I wanted to take a moment to thank the Tech Armor support team. Although this product wasn't suitable for me, they did refund this.----Couple of notes first:Had this one and iPhone 5 bought for me via my wish list, so although purchased via Amazon it will likely not show as verified purchase.This review is for the Privacy screen version, NOT the transparent one (Amazon appears to be coalescing the reviews) installed on a white iPad mini retina.To summarize:+ Easy to install when closely following directions+ Would likely protect screen from scratches+ At ~40 degree angle the screen is barely readable (good privacy), though not as total as 3M filters.+ Easy to remove. No sarcasm here, I was concerned that the adhesive may leave residue - it does not.- Does not completely cover iPad mini retina surface and would not recommend for white iPad (strangely enough the one shown in the product pictures)- Some vignetting of the image even when viewed from straight on (ie the image brightness reduces from center out), makes images / photos look unnatural.- The quality of the image shown overall is significantly less crisp with this filter on.Details:The installation of the protector was easy and went well.  The videos on the tech armor website are clear and concise and within 15 minutes I had both this one, and the iPhone 5 privacy screen installed with no bubbles, no fingerprints, and aligned as well as possible. There is still a 1-2mm gap on the left and right sides and ~1mm gap around the home button.  Looked a bit off as the dark filer contrasted with the white iPad surround, though acceptable.After installation, the initial image quality appeared significantly degraded.  Even taking into account that this is a privacy filter and so some direct-viewing light reduction is expected, setting the brightness to max (and trying auto-brightness on and off), the display was barely acceptable.Reading other reviews, and tech armor responses, I thought that a) I'd adjust to the screen and b) the the initial fuzziness would become less after 24 hours or so.I'm sad to say this was not the case.  It's now 4 days since installing this and I just had to remove it.  The brightness reduction I could tolerate, though the fuzziness completely negates the benefit of iPad retina and downgrades text quality to less than than original (non-retina) mini that my wife has.  This is the reason I have now removed this and thrown it away.I have photos of the same web page (Amazon) to allow compare / contrast - same device, same camera, same focusing distance, etc.I had hoped this would have worked as well as the 3M filter on my laptops, though unfortunately it didn't.  I hope others, including techarmor, can benefit from this review.If you have any questions or other feedback please leave a comment and I'll do my utmost to respond soon.  If you feel this review was not helpful, I'd doubly appreciate any feedback you can give on how to make it better, thanks.Cheers, Mike

Select a smaller unit, an alternate model or a different manufacturer for better performance; and do your due diligence in advance despite name brand reputation. I'm amazed that the other 7 reviewers had no problems.  I've tried installing this on 2 different computers: a desktop (XP) and a Toshiba Satellite laptop (Vista).  I hate to admit defeat on technology stuff, but I wasn't able to make it work on either.  Although the Amazon webpage suggests "J-Tech Digital" is the manufacturer, there's nothing about "J-Tech" on the box or in the documentation.  It's obviously generic stuff made in China or wherever.  Not that there's anything wrong with that.  The device does look like it's well made.  Several adapters and wires are included to help you out.  Everything looked so promising upon opening the box.  The problem seems to be with the software, which is provided by an outfit called "DisplayLink Graphics."  On each attempt to install, I followed their instructions precisely.  In each instance, the driver failed to install properly.  Right-clicking on the desktop after the "installation", as directed to do so, brought up nothing that had anything to do with DisplayLink.  All options in Display Properties continued to be exactly the same.  This was despite the fact that in Control Settings, Windows showed the software to be installed.  During the installation process, which literally lasts about 45 minutes, there were almost no windows telling me what was going on.  I like to be talked to during an installation.  Let me know you're still there and making progress.  I don't know why the installation of a graphics driver would have to take so long.  I can take a guess: poorly written code.  Trying to figure out if the process has been completed also isn't easy.  On a couple of occasions, I did see "Finished" somewhere in tiny font.  In the long run, I was never able to get get a second or alternate display.  BTW, I got this for my laptop to use during powerpoint presentations.  The Toshiba Satellite is equipped with low resolution graphics, and rather than have a new motherboard or graphics adapter installed, I was going to try for high definition output through an external device.  Also, in case you're wondering, I did not have the device connected during the initial installation (per the instructions), and I did uninstall the software before each attempt to re-install.  Uninstalling their software also takes forever.  I cannot recommend this device.  I'm returning it for a refund.UPDATE:  I waited a few days and tried again.  Still no luck.  I uninstalled the software (again) and used C-Cleaner to completely wipe away any hint of the software from the registry.  I meticulously followed their instructions.  First you install the software, and then you do a second level of installation with the hardware/display connected.  This time I noticed two advisories in the instructions warning that they will not tell you when either installation level is completed. So how are you supposed to know they're done???  They're not going to tell you.  You have to figure it out on your own.  Can't remember seeing that one before.  Also, the instructions do not exactly match up to what's shown on the screen.  Anyway, at one point, Vista told me that the installation was complete.  I checked the Vista Control Settings to make sure and then rebooted with the new display (Sony "Full HD" monitor) still connected via an HDMI jack.  Still nothing.  Although Vista shows the software to be installed, there is no hint of the software elsewhere, and in particular, nothing in Vista's Display Settings.  The instructions advise you to find their settings in Vista's Display Properties, or alternatively, by simply right-clicking on the desktop.  Again, I found absolutely nothing regarding their software in either place.  Maximum resolution was still 1280 x 860.  And, of course, the display connected to the device was blank.  So it's now officially on its way back to Amazon.

This is my first negative review of product that offers outstanding hardware. I bought this camera looking to expand upon the two rooms covered by my Foscam cameras. Overall I have been satisfied with my Foscam cameras, but was looking to expand beyond 720p resolution to 1080p offered by the Dropcam and have experienced some issues with the Foscam FW8921 model needing to frequently be restarted for the video feed to resume. The Dropcam Pro excelled in nearly every way over the Foscam with exception of one fatal flaw.PROs:*Fantastic aluminum build quality. Sleek and minimalistic design.*Setting port forwarding protocol through a router necessary to connect to the Foscam camera when away from home is a challenge. Setting up the Dropcam was a breeze, requiring only an IOS device and can be accomplished by anyone regardless of technological literacy.*Video quality both day and night are excellent. I was expecting the Dropcam Pro to provide a better picture offering more megapixels and full HD 1080p resolution in contrast to the 720p Foscam, but was still surprised at how much more clear the resolution appears.*Although the Dropcam does not feature pan and tilt, the wide field of view essentially eliminates the need of such feature.*There will be a video delay when viewing video broadcast from any Wi-Fi/IP camera. What is impressive about the Dropcam is it produces no longer delay than my Foscam cameras despite broadcasting in higher resolution and able to provide noticeable better frame rate at 1080p than the Foscam at 720p.CONs:*In order to capture a wide field of view the image does have a fisheye effect very similar to the video captured with action cameras.*Foscam and virtually all other IP cameras allow you to easily capture and record video or pictures either manually or setting up motion detection directly on your camera via an SD card, to your computer, or smartphone/tablet.  The only way Dropcam allows videos to be stored is through their cloud based storage. You will receive a short free trial then you get to add another recurring bill to your phone, internet, cable...etc bills, necessary to use this camera for any more than live (delayed) viewing. Additionally, Dropcam has done a good job at preventing customers implementing workarounds from paying for their cloud storage.Overall:$200 is a reasonable price for the build, image and overall performance quality this camera offers. Unfortunately, Dropcams efforts to keep cashing in on the product after the initial purchase is a horrendous approach taking advantage of customers and the reason mine was returned. Dropcam should entice consumers to use their cloud based storage through features such as superior application and website playback design not mandate in order to provide continued use of a product you purchased unsubsidized. The company intentionally prevents any means to record video through any method besides their cloud storage. Without paying the recurring fees the camera becomes practically useless. The delay in video and audio when viewing "live" makes it a poor choice as a baby monitor and without paying for recording capability it offers no surveillance value. I would strongly recommend waiting for Samsung to release their Smartcam HD model expected in March for $179 which match the features and design of Dropcam while adding local onboard storage eliminating privacy concerns and extra fees beyond initial price with the possible exception of an SD card. Hope this review is helpful. I provided all the highlights of the this product rather than simply complaining about my reason for returning for others to make an informed decision before purchasing. I am sure some will not mind the required recurring fee, but I feel the majority would choose otherwise if aware other options exists without the continued extra fees.*UPDATE*I have had 2 days to play around with the Samsung Smartcam HD and can gladly say so far it lives up to expectations combining the best of Foscam features with the top notch hardware of the Dropcam. The build quality of the Dropcam reigns supreme, like comparing Samsung Galaxy to an iPhone, but everything else is on par if not better with the Smartcam. Setup is just as simple on the Smartcam HD while offering the advantage of having the ability to setup straight from your Android phone or tablet in addition to iOS device. Load time to pull up the image on both cameras website and applications are nearly the same. Both cameras occasionally fail when attempting to connect from the Android app requiring a 2nd attempt. There is no clear winner in image quality with both offering nearly the same wide field of view, but somehow the Smartcam does so without as much of a fisheye effect. The mic and speaker on the Samsung are notably better. The Smartcam HD utilizes your Gmail account to send event (motion detection) notifications immediately to your phone and Picasa for snapshots of events, whereas the Micro SD slot is used to store video recordings. So if your worried about an intruder simply stealing the camera and all your evidence, then you will be relieved to have access of the free cloud storage of that photo of them taking the camera. Sure your limited to 1GB of free space on Picasa, but that stores a whole lot of images which are easy to delete straight from the Smartcam App. Unless you really need to have constant video recording being done, the Samsung Smartcam HD is a much better value that only increases as time passes and no furture bills become due. I plan on putting up a full review of the Smartcam HD once I have more time testing it out.

It is fantastic and is like having a new lens on your camera.The luminance denoising is good but I rate ACR slightly better, whereas the colour denoising is the best and better than ACR. Removal of colour aberrations is also the best, again because it is tailored to specific lenses.But I can say that it is the only raw processing software I have used/tried that was able to disguise banding noise I have on some GX10 images to the point where it was no longer intrusive.Local contrast adjustment is very good, the built 'HDR' adjustments are useful but watch out - they sometimes lower the colour impact of the image.The rest of the image adjustments are easy to use, there is wide range of preset colour tone adjustments and the end result, once you understand the software, is always a better picture. And it can do this automatically as well.But it falls down in three areas - firstly customer support is a bad joke - I've written to them numerous times about program crashes when trying out the trial of V7 on my old XP machine and never got a reply. Secondly, all adjustments are global i.e. they cover the whole image - there is no brush that you can use just on parts of the image. This is an irritation and sometimes a handicap.Lastly, it cannot handle converted DNG images, only original ones straight out of the camera - beware changing your images to DNG - they will be lost to this software.Although it can do jpeg images, it has limitations and I use it for raw only.V7 is faster than v6 but the image differences between the two versions is minimal for most pictures - at this stage, I'll stay with v6 since the benefits of changing are too small. But if you haven't used it before, give it a try - I did and my pictures are the better for it.

(I'd recommend it even at the same price as the Polk.) Don't let the price fool you; it's an excellent subwoofer, better than anything else out there for 2-3 times the price, and at this price, you could buy two of them instead of one Polk 505. Again, research that, and you'll find the unanimous view that the more subwoofers you have, the better. One is OK, but if you can afford it (and if you can afford one Polk 505 you can afford two Dayton Audio AUB-1200s!) buy two and place them in the middle of opposite walls (NOT the corners of the room unless you just want "boom" rather than accurate sound)(buy long Mediabridge subwoofer cables, too, to reach the subs if they're further away from your amp than your current cables will reach--another excellent value, btw). I guarantee that you will not be disappointed in the Daytons, and if you are, then you were not really in the market for a Polk 505; you wanted a $500-$600 subwoofer, which neither the 505 nor the Dayton Audio SUB-1200 is. reviewText: Although I own a laptop, I wanted something smaller and more portable for downloading pictures from my digital camera card when I'm traveling. That was my #1 reason for wanting a portable media player.I read a lot of reviews for the Digital Foci Picture Porter Elite and Epson P-5000 before deciding which one to buy.  My assessment was that the Epson was actually somewhat better (at almost twice the price); but the Picture Porter was also a very good choice.  My budget being what it is, I bought the 80Gb Picture Porter Elite from Amazon.  With their free shipping, Amazon had the best price I could find on the Internet.For my purposes, I stand by my decision to purchase the Picture Porter Elite.  On the other hand, I am neutral as to whether on not I would recommend this item to a friend.  That would really depend on how my friend intended to use it.Below is a list of things I consider to be pros/cons of the Picture Porter Elite.Accessories:(Pro) All of the cables you need for computer hook-up, television hook-up, audio/video copying, etc. are included. The unit also comes with a small remote control unit. The carrying case (also included; and actual leather, I think) is well made and has both a belt clip and carrying strap.(Con) The main unit is also used as the battery charger, which ties up the device while you recharge the battery.  (Note:  An external battery charger and spare battery is available if you want to spend the extra money.)Operating System, Control Buttons & Functions:(Pro) Downloading pictures from a memory card is quick and easy.  Just pop in a memory card and the backup menu appears automatically.  Choose the desired backup option, press "ok" with the joystick button, and the backup begins.(Con) The joystick button -- used to navigate, select a function, rotate photos, etc. -- is so tiny and overly sensitive that I find myself constantly choosing the wrong function with it.  Just as a side note, I'm a female with relatively small hands.  I imagine it would be much worse for a man with larger hands.  (Pro/Work-Around) You can choose to use the remote control instead on the onboard joystick.(Con) The operating system does not have built-in move or copy functions.  To perform these operations, you have to cut/copy the item and then paste it in the new location.  This is a slow and painful process!  Also, the operating system does not have a built-in function for creating a new folder.  (Pro/Work-Around) You can connect the Picture Porter to a desktop or laptop computer (via the supplied USB cable).  The computer will see the Picture Porter as a removable hard drive.  You can then use Windows Explorer to perform file and folder management functions, defrag the built in disk, etc.(Con) When viewing "portrait mode" photos, the picture porter DOES NOT automatically rotate the picture for you.  (Workaround) You can use the joystick or remote control to rotate the picture manually.Screen/Speakers:(Pro)  The screen resolution and image quality are very good ... even when zooming in on a photo.(Con) The screen is smaller than I expected.  The specs say 3.6"; but mind you, that is the diagonal screen measurement.  The actual screen is just under 3" wide.  Unless you have the eyesight of a hawk, the screen is really too small for watching videos/movies.(Con) The sound quality from the tiny built in speaker's is awful.  For decent sound, you have to use the earphones (included) or external speaker (not included).(Con) The earphones act as an antenna for the radio; so you can't listen to the radio without using them.Other Comments:Size & portable are relative.  This unit is by far preferable to lugging around a laptop; but it is not a tiny, fit in your jeans pocket, device.  In its case, the unit measures 5" wide x 3" tall x 1.75" deep and weighs just a fraction over 1 pound.Don't be fooled by all the "extra features" this media player has.  Aside from the ability to download directly from a memory card, and the massive storage capacity, most (if not all) of the features of this unit are available on a much smaller and less expensive MP3 player.  There is no way I would it carry this unit with me on a daily basis ... e.g. as my "brag book" for showing off pictures of my grandkids, or to listen to my MP3 music files.  It's just too bulky for that!  And, as I mentioned earlier, the screen is really too small to be a serious video/movie viewer.All things considered, if I had it to do over again, I'd buy the 40Gb model instead of the 80Gb.  I bought the 80Gb model in anticipation of using it as my photo "brag book" and music player; but as I mentioned above, it's really too bulky for that.I have tried to be honest and objective in my review of this product and I hope this helps you in making a decision whether or not to buy it.
summary: It's better than lugging a laptop; but ...

reviewText: I wanted to use this to wirelessly bridge my home theater set-up to my network.  My BluRay player has built-in 802.11g WiFi but the TV and Receiver only have ethernet.  Trying to stream full HD over 802.11g can be choppy; especially with microwave ovens and cordless phones about so while it is nice that the BluRay has wireless I really wanted something running 802.11n in the 5GHz band.  I didn't have too much difficulty getting the DAP-1533 to connect to my 802.11n access point, a D-Link DAP-2553, but that's where the joy ended as no device I connected to the DAP-1533 (including an old netbook running Ubuntu) could obtain an IP address via DHCP.  Sure, setting a static IP address worked but at this point in the evolution of home networking products I expect DHCP to work.I don't understand how D-Link could ship a product like this - it's just stupid.  I returned the DAP-1533 and instead opted for an Actiontec MoCA adapter. Once the MoCA adapter arrived I was done setting everything up in 30 minutes with all three devices plugged into an old 8-port hub I had - no wireless configuration nonsense - done!

reviewText: Well, this product seems so futuristic - Streaming audio from PC, Internet Radio, Rhapsody ..., yet the shortcomings in some of these features make this unit not up to the mark. I've had this computer for almost two years now. I bought this laptop so that I could take notes more easily on campus, since I have problems note-taking by hand. My first Inspiron, a 1505, was a tank that still runs like a dream, but I thought it was time for an upgrade, so I went with another Dell. I use this computer only occasionally, as I have a desktop. For the amount of use it's gotten, I'm surprised at how quickly it is falling apart.The first problem I had with this computer was my Windows 7 upgrade CD. My CD was shipped defective, so I called Dell customer service (not recommended) and they told me that I was not eligible for the upgrade. Why do I have the CD then? Many calls later, I finally got them to agree to send a new CD. They sent me, I kid you not, printer software. Does Dell even make printers? I threw myself back into the customer service circus, and finally walked away with my upgrade after FOUR MONTHS.The first time my computer's outer shell cracked, I sent it back to Dell for replacement, as I was still under warranty. This is a part that I could easily replace myself. Dell said that was not possible. They assured me that they did not need to wipe my hard drive for this procedure. Guess what? They did it anyways!Again, the back shell of my computer began to break. This time, I was out of warranty. I didn't slam my laptop around or really do anything damaging to it. It just decided to crack one day when I closed the lid. Now, it is completely broken apart. I have had to become very creative with duct tape. My down key started malfunctioning not long after that. It became stuck constantly in the down position, making it impossible to type. The key itself was not stuck down. I had to take the key off to prevent this. Today, my disk drive cover fell off.I'm not really sure what is wrong with the touch pad for this computer, but I've been told other people have problems too. Randomly, the cursor jumps all over the screen. Sometimes, the touch pad doesn't work at all. Sometimes, it resizes the page you are viewing for no reason.Dell has manufactured their laptops to work only with Dell A/C adapters, which is a real tragedy. My adapter gave up the ghost right after my warranty ran out. Of course, Dell wants an astronomical sum for a replacement. If you buy a far superior and more reliable off-brand adapter, it may connect to your computer, but it probably will not charge your battery. Congratulations! Your once-convenient laptop is now a slightly smaller desktop. My adapter, oddly, will charge my computer sometimes, but not at other times.This computer is crash-happy. Mine crashed twice, both during final exams. I lost TONS of data on the first crash. It also includes horrible McAfee. Be prepared to hunt down a program designed specifically for uninstalling this antivirus, because it can really mess your computer up.My husband bought an HP around the same time I bought this Dell. It is still going strong. Next time, I guess I'll know what to go with instead.

Although this laptop looks beautiful and is very thin and light, potential purchasers must be warned of some potentially deal-breaking problems.The main problem is this: The laptop has stealthy "sharp edges". I put "sharp edges" in quotation marks because the edges feel fine when you run your fingers over them, but when you are using the laptop with your wrists resting on the edge, you will occasionally feel a very sharp pinch or cut on your skin (enough to shock you and make you jerk your hands up in pain). It seems like this is caused by the very minute crevice that runs along the edge of the laptop. On paper, this sounds like a minor annoyance but in practice, it is a MAJOR problem because I find myself not being able to use my laptop naturally and in peace - I have to either elevate my wrists while typing, place tissue paper underneath them, or be constantly worried about when the next pinch will come.Another major problem that is not specific to this laptop is the fact that many apps and programs are not designed for ultra high definition screens. Words and icons appear far too small when running this laptop on its native resolution, and it is virtually unusable unless you change the DPI scaling to maximum. Yet playing with the DPI scaling also messes up some programs (for e.g. text might get cut off from a window that cannot be resized). In the end I find myself dialing down the screen resolution to 1080p, which completely defeats the purpose of paying a premium for a QHD screen.Other minor annoyances include:- The Power button is located beside the Delete button (in the place where the Delete button of most other laptops would be). You might find yourself accidentally hitting the Power button and shutting down your laptop when all you wanted to do was to hit Delete.- Because of the laptop's thinness, key travel on its keyboard is slightly less than what I have been used to on other laptops.- Only 2 USB ports- The laptop was quite laggy at normal web browsing at first. The lag only went away after using the laptop for a few weeks. I've no idea why - perhaps it was due to the lack of some drivers that were eventually installed by Windows Update?- There is an annoying Virtual Keyboard icon that keeps appearing in the taskbar no matter what I do to try to remove it or disable it permanently. This seems to be a problem with how Asus configured the laptop because I have attempted many fixes that worked for other people, with no success.I will also add one thing about battery life - the battery life of this laptop, and Haswell laptops in general, is rather overrated. My previous laptop (ASUS UL30Vt), which I bought four years ago, had a 12-hour battery life, and even after four years the battery still lasts for a decent 8 hours. This laptop's battery life is about 6-8 hours, which is a step down, and yet there is no noticeable improvement in performance for day-to-day activities like web browsing (in fact, as I've already mentioned, it was laggier than my old laptop initially)For these reasons, I very much regret purchasing this laptop, and would urge any potential purchaser to look elsewhere.

reviewText: This is the third iPod, and 2nd iPod touch I have owned.  While I generally love the iPod products (I have bought three after all!), because I like their interface and how they work, I have been particularly unhappy with my latest iPod touch.  I bought this 4th generation iPod with the IOS 5 back in October 2011, when it was just released.  The first thing I noticed was that while 8 GB was more than ample on my old (2nd gen) iPod Touch, with the new OS, I am constantly having to worry about what apps, music and podcasts I can and cannot sync, because my 8 GB is always close to full (I used to have like 2.5 GB free without worry, and now I fight to have 0.5 GB free).  I don't know if it is because of the iPod being so close to full, or if it just has these problems, but I also have more issues with nonresponsiveness or sluggishness in opening apps, etc.  In addition, on my old iPod touch the auto-brightness really worked.  I could use one very dim brightness setting, and could see the screen both at night in my dark bedroom,  and also out in the daylight at noon.  On this 4th gen iPod touch I literally have to change the brightness setting twice a day, so I can see it during the day, but not be blinded at night.  And the real kicker (if that wasn't all enough), is that the 4th gen iPod is extremely breakable!!!  I don't know if I was spoiled with the 2nd gen model or what, but apparently the new model simply can't put up with being dropped hardly at all.  I haven't done anything I didn't do to my old iPod, and while I had it 2 years with no major damage (despite being dropped dozens of times), in just 10 months I have completely destoyed the screen and frame on the 4th gen iPod.  Two of the corners are completely shattered, and another is crumpled so that you can see inside the iPod.  On one of the shattered corners a big chunk of glass has broke off.  I have a network of about 5 major cracks through the length of screen.  I guess the amazing part (besides how fragile the darn thing is), is that is still works with the screen in pieces.  When you look at the profile of the iPod touches, in the 2nd Generation, the metal frame went up around the glass.  In the 4th generation the glass lays above the level of the metal frame; I am guessing this is why is is so fragile.  I guess in the future I will know to look out for this.  I haven't ruled out buying another iPod touch (I do like them -[am I crazy?]), but I think I will be a more astute buyer in the future.  I will look at where the glass lays in relation to the frame (and probably get a protective case no matter what).  And this time if my auto-brightness or something doesn't work, I am taking the iPod back right away, and not wait until I have cracked the thing up and probably voided any warranty.

I purchased this controller card with the intention of switching my system/boot drive over to a SSD. As my motherboard only has SATA II ports, to maximize the data transfer speed of the SSD I knew I would have to use a SATA III add-on card. I was aware that since this was going through a PCIe x1 slot I wouldn't be able to achieve full SATA III speeds, but since my motherboard's PCIe slots are 2.0 compliant, it should have been able to approach 500 MB/s.  I knew there was a possibility that this card was not bootable, but as it wasn't too expensive and that it provided an USB 3.0 port as well, I figured I'd give it a try.  Even if I wasn't able to boot from it, I'd still have an use for it.  Trying to find information on what PCIe SATA III cards are bootable is rather difficult - I was only able to verify for certain that a few boards have that capability, and that was mainly from reading user reviews and forums and not from info provided by the manufacturers and vendors.  So here's the breakdown on this card:Pros:o Not too expensiveo Provides an USB 3.0 porto Comes with a SATA cableCons:o Not bootableo Poor quality internal SATA connectoro Terrible data transfer speeds and integrityo Comes with a SATA cableThe SATA cable I used is a high-quality SATA III certified cable with a metal locking clip and not the generic one provided; however it did not fit snugly on the connector on the card and it was very easy to pull it loose.  After installing the card and the drivers, when I connected my SSD I was was able to format and access it OK.  However, when I attempted to clone my HD to the SSD, the software I was using reported a data integrity error and aborted.  Just to make sure my new SSD wasn't at fault, I connected it to one of the motherboard's SATA II ports and I was able to clone the drive no problem.  Just for giggles I tried the provided SATA cable, but it wouldn't even recognize the SSD was plugged in. I updated the firmware on the card, tested it again, and then updated the drivers and did some additional testing.  I used HD Tach to test data transfer speeds, and this is what I found:WHEN I was able to complete a test with HD Tach using the IOCrest card (it would often give me an error or just lock up) the SSD was only able to achieve data transfer speeds of approximately 105 MB/s.  My primary HD connected to an onboard SATA II port gave me around 244 MB/s, and the SSD on an onboard port was clocking in at 263 MB/s which is getting close to the maximum transfer rate of SATA II.  Of course testing using a benchmarking program only gives you synthetic results, but as you can see there is something very wrong with this card.This card uses the ASMedia ASM104x host controller.  Apparently there was an ASM1041, but if you go to ASMedia's website they only list their ASM1042 "Universal Serial Bus 3.0 extended host controller".  No where in the specifications does it state that it is also a SATA controller; it specifically says it's a PCI Express USB Host controller.  So that makes me wonder if the manufacturer of the card (which is Syba by the way; IOCrest & Syba are the same company, which explains why all their product numbers are the same) isn't trying to make this particular chip and controller board do something that it really wasn't designed to do.  Here's the link to ASMedia's specifications on the ASM1042:[...] (Sorry, Amazon strips out URLs even if it isn't a product link... you'll just have to do a search on your own; I tried. :) )As a matter of fact when you install the drivers for this card, it only shows up as a ASMedia XHCI Controller under USB controllers in Device Manager.  It does not appear as a Storage Controller or an IDE ATA/ATAPI controller, which again makes me conclude this particular chip is being used for something other than what it was intended for.  Obviously this isn't ASMedia's fault, but rather Syba/IOCrest's as the manufacturer of the controller card.Since I don't currently have an USB 3.0 device to connect to the card, I can't tell you how it performs to that extent, but as a SATA controller it's useless.  I took a chance and lost.  Hopefully I can prevent others from making the same mistake.
summary: Piece of garbage - do not waste your money!

Also, the red-eye reduction and face finder features typically cause my son to shut his eyes for every picture.  I have some lovely shots of him napping, but that's about it.  If you are shooting landscapes or other photos where your subjects will remain still, then this camera is probably fine.  However, I wouldn't recommend it for folks trying to photograph small children or animals.  Additionally, I've found the video mode to be disappointing as well.  The videos have all been surprisingly dim, considering they weren't taken in low-light environments.  Perhaps I received a dud, but I won't be purchasing another Nikon camera. I've been working with Wacom tablets since the early '90s and the history of poor behavior between computer and tablet would be comical if not so painful. You would think for the money they charge for these, and the length of time this company has been around, they would hire some competent engineers.New Mac Book Pro, new tablet, installed driver and got to work with the tablet pretty quickly. The touch behavior took some getting used to, drag never worked, but everything else was an amusing novelty that worked essentially as advertised. Don't like the buttons in the corners, the tend to trigger a lot when I'm typing. Disabled them. Touch is cool, again it'll trigger if you're typing so I turn it on and off. I would probably go with the pen-only tablet if I were to re-purchase, touch is not really necessary for my workflow.2 days into using the device, I needed to plug my iPhone into the USB port to set up wifi sync. Unplugged the Wacom, got the iPhone synced and plugged the Wacom back in. Dead. Ok, restart the machine, it's not the first time I've seen Wacom drivers get confused. Still dead. Shut down Mac, fire back up. Still dead. WTF? Meh. Here we go again....reinstall driver, no response. Uninstall driver, reinstall driver, restart, multiple incarnations of same, no response from the tablet. Check the cord, totally seated correctly in the tablet and Mac ports. Check the USB port on the Mac, it recognizes the iPhone, so it is still functional. Plug the tablet into another Mac Book Pro running the same OS as the new one, no response from the tablet. Install tablet driver, still no response from the tablet. Change out cord, no response from the tablet. Look all over the tablet, no reset button. This thing is just dead, apparently for the sin of hot swapping it out for another device. Nice.Wacom support? Let's just say "good luck with that". Ok, off to Google to see what I can find. Seems USB power problems are known on these things for a few different reasons. People send them back to Wacom and get them back after the few months that it takes to fix the problem, then they die again after a short period of time (2 months, a few weeks, a few days, etc.). Apparently a work around is to buy the $40 wireless dongle, but this has been reported to have issues as well.Sorry, nope, I don't have time for that nonsense. This tablet is part of the way I make my living, I can't wasted time repeatedly trying to troubleshoot it, and then send it back to the company to be without it for weeks or months.Incidentally, the Intuos 2 that I've been using for years works fine on the new machine. I had to uninstall the pen and touch tablet driver, then install the Intuos 2 legacy driver, but it works as expected. I want to move the old Mac out to my photography studio and put the Intuos 2 out there with it, which is why I purchased a new tablet. The new tablet is log and the reviews out there on the Interwebs indicate mine is not a one-off, so this brick is going to be returned and I'll find another old tablet on ebay.Wacom, once again, you suck at new hardware and you suck at drivers. Purchasing Wacom products is always a crap shoot and using them tends to be a matter being a capable troubleshooter with every OS upgrade. Some of that is to be expected, but it just happens far too often with these things. Hardware is suppose to be transparent and it is suppose to just work, a long history with Wacom products proves that a company can continue to exist without quality products. When they work, they're great, too bad they are so inconsistent with that functionality feature.
summary: Typically horrible Wacom experience - dead tablet after 2 days

I've been looking for a replacement for my admittedly unloved Logitech Pure-Fi Elite for some time. Found the iP1 at a certain well-known warehouse chain for a great price due to an instant discount promotion, but also saw the intriguing Panasonic SC-HC3 alongside it on the shelf. Decided to buy both and have a shoot-out testing session at home, with the loser going back to the store. Not a true apples-to-apples comparison, since the SC-HC3 is really more a compact stereo than dedicated speaker setup, but since I was primarily after was great sound quality in a package that had some style and 'look at me' presence, there was considerable leeway on my part in rooting for the iHome unit.Unfortunately for the iP1, the SC-HC3 does sound exceptionally well also. In fact, to my ears even better than what the iP1 is capable of. It also has good looks, too. The iP1's frequency range is pretty good, with decent and relatively convincing midbass performance for the size drivers it has onboard. Mids and highs are present, but I found that they seemed conspicuously muted with passages that I know shouldn't be that way when listened to on other equipment and setups. I used my 2G Touch as the source iPod, and used lossless WAV files across several musical genres; the iP1 is certainly the best-sounding iHome unit I've ever experienced, and the best-looking to my tastes as well. But I found the abrupt crossover from mid/woofer to tweeter too noticeable and rather irritating to listen to over time (on my unit this was really apparent with the right channel), and there wasn't much in the way of depth or image to its sound at all, not that I was holding out much hope considering that the respective drivers for each channel are mounted less than a foot apart from one another. But in the end it was the balance of the sound across the frequency range that bugged me the most.In usage I found that I preferred using the iP1's digital processing circuitry over leaving it off and presumably neutral; it brought a liveliness and level of resonance to the audio that made the unboosted output seem bland, inconsequential and haphazard, which is actually contrary to how I usually like my music with other equipment that offer similar forms of 'tarting'. Simply stated, overall I found the iP1's sonic presentation decent, but just not as accurate as I would normally prefer. The imbalance I felt with midrange and high frequency output and the harsh crossover point from the midrange/woofer to tweeter introduced too much distracting characteristics to the sound, and the lack of depth when compared to the Panasonic's sonic performance put the iP1 at a distinct disadvantage to my ears.From an aesthetic view, the broadbrush overview of the iP1 makes it look a winner that cater to my design preferences, but even here there are quirks as well. The power supply is external and is the poster child of the prodigal power 'brick'; it's about as big as the one that Microsoft supplies with the Xbox 360, and is cumbersome to place, conceal and plan around when locating the iP1 in the intended resting spot I had in mind for it...just like I experienced and loathed with the old Pure-Fi Elite I was so intent on replacing. In fact it's probably worse since the iP1 is see-through.The smoked acrylic front face and the general finish of the speaker drivers is minimalist stylish in my mind's eye (though my wife hated it), but the materials used on the dock tray fascia and control surfaces seemed a bit low end in comparison. The overall effect is entrancing, but this design would've really been fantastic had iHome used tempered glass and metal on the remaining plastic surfaces, but I suspect the $300 list price would be a fair bit higher as a result. From the rear, the housings for the speaker drivers and miscellaneous electronics also seemed a bit on the cheap side as well, though in truth all they do is sit in the background since they're primarily viewed through the main acrylic face panel. There were a couple of fascia treatment options for the midrange/woofer driver supplied: the metal mesh grilles come pre-installed from iHome, with separate plastic bezel trim rings also included that give the iP1 owner the choice to expose the mid/woofer speaker driver. Since the grilles are supposedly acoustically neutral, the trim ring accessory would only be used as an aesthetic preference. Personally, I think the grilles work better from a visual standpoint, since the tweeters also are sheathed with a similar mesh that isn't removable.In the end, the iHome iP1 lost my impromptu shoot-out with the Panasonic SC-HC3. The added features of the Panasonic (AM/FM, CD player, clock) along with its Bang & Olufsen-esque styling and its far cheaper price--even with the instant discount on the iP1 at the time of purchase, the iP1 is almost 50% more expensive than the SC-HC3--simply outshone the stylish iHome unit and underscored the value aspect in this comparison. And in these tough economic times, that last point alone makes the one-trick pony iP1 a harder horse to ride. Couple the Panasonic's ability to provide me with superior and pleasing audio performance (your own mileage may vary, however), it was clear to me which of the two was going back to the store.I think that the iP1 is a good first effort by iHome at trying to reach into the higher-quality segment of the iPod speaker/dock market that others like Bose and Klipsch play in, but for me the expertise and know-how of old-school manufacturer Panasonic won out on this day. Maybe next time, iHome.
summary: Good but not the greatness I had hoped for

If you want a real PVR option, don't buy this card.  Buy the video card and TV card separately.  I've had an AIW card for a year and wish I had spent a few extra bucks 11 months ago.Don't get me wrong.  I have another computer equipped with a 9800 Pro without the AIW features.  It's an excellent card.  I'm still using the AIW card in this machine, but only as a video card, not as a TV tuner...and it works just fine.The idea behind a video capture card is that you can pause, rewind and record live TV.  By far the best way to do this is to buy a separate video capture card with hardware encoding.  This way, the card converts the video signal into a format that can be saved on your hard drive (mpeg2).Otherwise, your CPU must do the work.  That's what ATI All-in-Wonder cards do.  While ATI makes great video cards, integrated cards like the AIW cards rely on the CPU to do all the dirty work.Video is somewhat jerky when you have TIVO capabilities enabled (pause/rewind live TV).  You'll notice it especially when watching sports -- because the card drops frames due to the heavy CPU load.Their TV software is pretty decent -- and actually has some pretty great features.But their guide software (Guide Plus+) leaves much to be desired.  You have to manually iniate guide updates and it only downloads the guide a week at a time -- so you have to remember to update the guide.  Other available packages download the guide automatically, daily, and two weeks at a time.I have an AMD Athlon 2600 CPU with 512 MB of RAM and two 80GB hard drives and I still encountered all these problems.  I spent a year trying to get better performance and finally broke down and bought a card with hardware encoding (the Avermedia UltraTV 1500 MCE).  I now have two 1500 MCE cards installed in the same machine...and the performance is still much better than the single AIW card.  I can record one show and watch another, or record two shows.  Still, pause/rewind live TV works flawlessly.The picture is better, the sound is better, TIVO capabilities work without compromising system performance or dropping frames.  I started using Snapstream BeyondTV software to view and record shows and I couldn't be happier.In short, spend an extra $20 and skip the video/TV tuner combo cards and you'll be much happier in the long run.

When a product description does not clearly identify a product as either new or used, it is to be assumed that it is new.  I therefore ordered two of these batteries.  They both performed as though they were well used batteries that were almost beyond their useful service life, rather than like new product.To establish the comparison, I recently purchased some additionalVTech CS6209handsets to expand my cordless system beyond the original two I purchased it with.  The new handsets with stock batteries last longer between charges, don't take as long to fully charge, and they can produce enough power to operate the screen backlight when reporting a low charge.  By contrast, the older handsets using this battery require more frequent charges, take longer to fully charge, and stop being able to light the screen BEFORE it reports low battery.  This describes how the original batteries with those initial handsets performed in the last few months prior to completely dying.This is nothing like I expected, as these batteries are labeled as 800 mAh (milliampere-hours, a rating of power over time; larger numbers represent longer usage time), and the stock batteries are rated for 500 mAh.  These SHOULD therefore last longer; they do not.

According to the discussion I read, this is an issue Fintie is working to resolve.  I'm sure that will help those in the future who buy this case, but it really doesn't do a whole lot to make me happier.[edit: It seems Fintie and Amazon might be pointing fingers at each other here on the above problem, but it also seems to me that the actual fault was not with the original design of the case, but with an Amazon software update.  Regardless of whose fault it may be, the problem exists.  Fintie, in a form-letter type reply to this review, posted a 'temporarily solution' which, having tried it, seems to me to be far more trouble than just using a different case, even if I didn't have other issues with the case, which they completely ignored in the form response.]Finally, I've been using this case now less than a full day (about 22 hours, 9 of which I was sleeping, and 8 of which I was working), and the cover no longer turns the device on when you open it, which isn't a big deal to me, nor does it turn the device off when you close the cover, which *is* a big deal to me.If my only choices were to use this case or no case at all...it'd be a tough call. I bought the Sansa Express to replace a Creative MuVo that had a worn-out play button after one year of heavy use (and flawless performance).  The features I liked (and still like) about the Sansa Express were its 1) small size, 2) micro SD expandability to 3 GB, 3) FM recorder, and 4) ability to plug, sync and charge directly in a USB port.  I didn't care about seeing pictures, album art, etc. on a tiny screen.Soon after I started using the device, however, performance problems became more than a nuisance.  The biggest problem is that the device frequently freezes for no apparent reason when the controls are used.  The only way to restore it to responsiveness is to perform a cold re-set of the device.  This loses your playing "place" and also zaps all your FM pre-sets.  Also, the re-set procedure will only work if you first eject the micro SD card, and then it must be re-inserted afterwards (at which point the contents of the card are re-indexed which in itself takes an inconvenient amount of time).  I downloaded the most recent firmware for the device on 7/4/2007, and it failed to correct this problem.  I have since learned that the surprise freeze feature is not uncommon with this device.Other problems seem to be present by design.  For example, the fully-seated micro SD card protrudes about 1mm beyond the body of the device.  The SD card will occasionally eject accidentally when another object taps it and triggers the ejection spring.  So far I have not lost a card, but it is only a matter of time.The pause feature is annoying, in that the paused device completely shuts down after about 15 seconds, losing its place in the file you were listening to and returning to the beginning.  This is not a problem when you are in the middle of a 3-minute song, but it is a big problem when you are 45 minutes into a 1-hour podcast.I was forewarned about the display's visibility problems when one is outdoors, so I can't complain too harshly about that, except to say that it was even worse than I expected.  The display is completely invisible in all but the most shaded outdoor areas.All in all, the device has been a disappointment.  Even with the design flaws, I would have recommended it were it not for the surprise freeze feature.  Because of that feature, however, I must recommend that the buyer look elsewhere for a flash .mp3 player with similar features.UPDATE: 7/27/2007.  I contacted customer support and they arranged to ship back the old and give me a new, non-defective unit.  I have had it for a week or so now and so far it has frozen just once in an unusual situation. It has performed extremely well during routine use.  Thumbs up to Sandisk's customer support operation.  I must give credit where it is due!  If Amazon makes it possible, I am changing my rating from 2 stars to 4.  (It is not a 5 because of the aforementioned design problems... invisible display, unreasonably brief pause feature, and microSD protrusion.)
summary: Disappointed and frustrated (but now have non-defective unit!)

Okay, this thing was going to have to perform some serious acrobatics to take the place of its older brother, the Harmony One universal remote control. I have been using the Harmony One for quite a while, the better part of a year and I was happy. It was simplicity itself to setup and use.The 1100 came packaged in Logitech's usual bullet-proof packaging. I have to admit right off that I really liked the initial look of it. Installing the included software was, as usual, easy. Programming the unit involved plugging it into the computer via an included USB cable and entering the makes and models of the various electronica you wish to control through an easy-to-use interface.That part was easy enough, but I was somewhat inconvenienced by having to open yet another account with Logitech to setup the remote. My "old" account I had for the Harmony One could no  longer be used. I mean, it's not the end of the world, but I wish I didn't have to set up two Logitech accounts simply because I had two Logitech remote controls.After software setup, the unit's easy enough to figure out. As promised, the touch screen is wonderful and bright and, surprisingly fast. I touched the fast-forward button three times in rapid succession and bam! bam! bam! the remote sent out three commands to the DVR without a fuss. Definitely rapid response, something I'm over the moon about.Use drains the batteries rather quickly and certainly quicker than the Harmony One which does have a smaller screen so that's understandable but I find I need to have the 1100 in the charger more often now.Another usage quirk that I have been able to overcome only with some difficulty is what I can only call the "no-look" control. With most remote controls I have used, I come to recognize by feel which buttons I have to press for the various controls I require. Soon, I can work the remote control in the dark, one hand working the controls and one draped over my lovely wife. Quite a feat, if I say so myself.However, there's no such facility with the 1100. Because there are no buttons per se, one has to peer closely over the screen to make sure of the area one is pecking at, but I'm hoping that with time it gets easier. As it is currently, I still have to bring the device into view and, using both hands now (one holding the 1100 and the other touching buttons), using the 1100 takes more time than does the Harmony One. Another rather annoying thing is that I sometimes have to shake the 1100 senseless to make the screen re-appear after it goes into blank screensaver mode.I have also found that with the devices I have, the default setup programming leaves out a lot of functions. So for example, the DVR controls have the usual pause, stop, play, and so on buttons on the main screen, but leaves out the 15-second rewind and the 30-second fast-forward and others. There are empty slots that can be programmed in so they perform those functions, but I wish those were in place by default.The 1100 is a really good remote control, but there are enough disadvantages from using some of Logitech's older remote controls that I cannot give this one my highest recommendations. However, it is good enough to garner 4 stars out of 5.*Update: March 10, 2010. I've been using the Harmony for quite a while now and it's gotten easier to use, however something very annoying has cropped up: an electronic whine revs up once the LCD screen comes on. It's loud enough that it makes using the remote a teeth-gritting experience. I'm going to demote it to 3 stars.
summary: Superb Construction, Slightly Difficult To Use

Apex DVD players are made for the most budget conscious of consumers, but my philosophy on buying electronics stands firm: If you're going to get one, spend a little extra and get a good one. The Apex AD-1200 is a tough recommendation even at the low price.The strength of this DVD player is simple: It plays DVDs. For people who will only watch a DVD occasionally, that is not a problem. It offers good picture quality and decent sound quality. Surprisingly, it plays VCDs and MP3s rather well, which means that those burned CDs that won't work on your stereo will most likely work here. Basically, you can expect a minimal level of performance from this particular DVD player.But the problems with this model are plentiful. The biggest flaw is the design. This DVD player is light, and feels cheap. Note the absence of a digital display on the player. Also, repeated pushing of the buttons can result in them falling out, so be careful of how hard you press the buttons. Worse yet, the player is loud and clunky. This clicks, hums, and rattles all through the movie. It is like a CD-ROM trying to read the disk.Having said that it is functional is not so true in the long term. As you would expect from a lower-end appliance, the Apex DVD player will stop working properly after a while. Often, the picture will freeze while the player tries to read the disk, and there are certain DVDs that it cannot read at all. This is a big annoyance, and a good reason to steer clear of this player.Buying a DVD player is never an easy decision, but choosing one strictly for the price is not a good idea. Most likely, you'll spend more having to buy a new one to replace the Apex brand when it breaks down. Spend a few extra bucks and get a good one instead, and avoid the headaches.
summary: Basically, you get what you pay for.

Usually it doesn't tip over anymore. A minor point, but still, I appreciate the added stability. The grip controls fall naturally to hand. Having the wheel and the adjustment buttons located where they are makes for tweaking the settings and taking the photo from a vertical position an easy process now. Both battery trays lock firmly and solidly in place. It comes with an IR remote and an LCD display, both which seem to be of limited usefulness.  All in all, I appreciate the added size and heft the grip provides (I don't mind the extra weight, in fact I don't care for overly light cameras -- they tend to jitter some when heavier cameras won't). It has made for a much more comfortable picture-taking experience.Now for the Cons:The LCD display is about to get on my last nerve.  I have repeatedly set the clock and calendar, only to discover sometime later (days or weeks?) that it's way off. Again.  And because the controls to set it are not intuitive at all, I get to either futz around with it for way to long trying to figure out how to get it into "set" mode, have to dig out the Chinglish manual, whose meaning is entirely too opaque, or I just forget about it. I don't much need a 24 hour ONLY clock anyway, or a calendar that is in YYMMDD format. Thanks to the reviews here, I'm more appreciative of the "lock" function, which I have now insured is engaged. Let's see if this takes care of the problem. I still suspect my grip has a defective clock/calendar function.I too have experienced the spontaneous and apparently random triggering of the camera. First time it happened was a couple of weeks ago. I didn't know what was going on, whether my camera was defective, or the grip? Finally, it stopped firing when I shut the grip off. Since then it hasn't misbehaved, and after reading through some of the posts here, I think I know what caused it. Apparently the IR sensor will self-trigger in bright sun situations -- but not all? I was using it in a bright sun situation when it began to fire randomly, but I also used it in an even brighter bright sun situation more recently, and it didn't misfire at all. So I remain somewhat puzzled. But if there's a way to disable this "feature" I will do so. Gotta go dig out the Chinglish manuals again . . .About battery life: I haven't monitored it that closely, but it does seem to be a bit on the high side.  After about a month of little if any use, I went to pick it up a couple weeks ago only to find the onboard rechargables totally dead.  Which seemed odd. So, not having time to recharge them (I was headed out the door), I loaded up the AA tray with alkalines and was on my way. I found myself being very thankful for the AA tray at that point.  So I do the shoot -- my daughter's college graduation -- which amounted to maybe 400 photos (including about 200 random ones, thanks to the IR wierdness), and notice a few days later that the battery indicator was down to one bar.  Then this past weekend, I grabbed the camera for another shoot and headed out, without thinking about the battery condition. I made it through this shoot -- probably about 50 images all told -- and the inidicator is still at one bar.  So it almost seems as if it drains the juice quickly but that once it's drawn it down most of the way, it doesn't suck it down as fast.  I dunno.  I need to pay closer attention to this -- but with my rechargables, since draining 6 AA alkalines at a time gets kinda expensive.I'm glad I found out from the other reviews here that the random firing is due to the IR function. Now that I know what is causing it, I feel I may be able to deal with it better. Still, if I had it to do all over again, I think I'd save a few bucks and buy the grip without the LCD. Not only will the aggravation level be reduced, but the battery life will likely be increased.
summary: Nice, but not without its quirks

reviewText: This is my original review. According to my own experience, you have a 1 in 3 chance of receiving a cheap batch.  I have posted my revised review below this one, in case you don't like those odds.I have a lot of cd's. Almost all of them will only see occasional use. For those cd's, I have these. For the ones that get frequent use, I get the slim cases. The current price for these come out to 4 cents per piece, while the more durability- but 4-5x's as thick-"thin" cd holders average around 24-26 cents, and that's IF you buy them here. Hopefully, Amazon didn't delete the price. If they did, the cases come out to 6 x's the price of the sleeves. Someone suggested these were more durable at office depot and were "slightly" more expensive. Well, point me to that office depot, because I remember them just as thin and for 2 and half times the price. So, to each his/her own, but if I happen to get some that have the window sliding off, it's OK. (I'm excluding the reviewer who said all the windows were sliding off; obviously got a defective purchase) Would I like to have all of them be durable and never rip, sure; but keep in mind that 100 come in a pack, so....some are going to rip. If you purchase 100 of anything other than expensive products which go through a rigorous inspection process (and even still...), you'll more than likely be just as ticked off at the result. Let me just say though that I haven't had a single one rip or tear and I'm on my second purchase of these. If someone thinks these are a replacement for cd cases where they can keep pulling and putting the cd's back in the sleeve without ever having ripping problems, they'll be disappointed. These are mainly for storing and occasional use, along with preventing your cd's from scratching while not in use. In the end, I'm a big "quality is everything" person, but so is price, if that's even possible. Let's make it possible so I don't have to change my nifty quote. One note: you will have to fold the flap of each one down before you put it in the sleeve. I don't remember if this was required with the office depot, but the reviewer who mentioned his purchase there didn't state whether he/she had to or not. There's a crease already stamped into the sleeve, so it isn't hard. You'd be saving 6 cents for every 2 seconds it takes you to fold it, which works out to 6 bucks for 3.3 minutes of work. I don't make 109 bucks an hour, so I'll fold them myself if this happens to be the case.Revised Review:After receiving the first two batches I ordered (ordered at least a month apart from each other), I went ahead and ordered another batch. Immediately upon grabbing the first sleeve in order to fold the top, I felt dirt, or what I thought was perhaps dust from the warehouse they may have come from. After my 5th one in I also noticed the sleeve was a little "darker" than I was used to and also there was a very slight wave to the sleeves I hadn't seen before. After a closer inspection, I got slightly depressed. I actually need these now, but now I have to reorder from another seller. It turns out that these ARE NOT made by the first people who manufactured my first two batches, and are far cheaper. The first sleeves I received previously had a smooth feel to them, there was no warping of the sleeve (due to cheapness of the paper, I presume), the paper was thicker (I assumed these were darker, because I was actually seeing my brown desk underneath them while folding the tops), and even the tab punches that are made to fold the top into in order to seal the top are different. I put the tabs of one I had left over from before and held it up next to the ones from this batch, and the difference in quality was stark. The punches made on these latest sleeves left a jagged curve that didn't even cut all the way through. I NEVER had to press a finger through the tab in order to get it to fully open on the last batch, and here I am having to take extra seconds just to make sure the tabs will open without having to manually open them. Unacceptable. A company should never produce a product in two different places KNOWING FULL WELL that the quality of the product differs so much between the two places. I've always hated that practice and there's no exception here. Many of these reviews, I'm sure, are for the first type of sleeves I received, and it is dishonest, or at best, moronic to assume that it is ok to pull-what is in my opinion-a form of "bait-and-switch" on your customers. Not ok. I will not hand these things to customers/clients and will only suggest these for the purposes of storing away rarely used disks. I would much rather pay a couple bucks extra for the quality of the first two batches then settle on these. For me, it would have still been worth the price. But these? Will be returned to Americopy, so they can include this into their company's "how can we cut costs" debate. One-star, Americopy, for switching the quality on me. Go sit in the corner and think about what you've done.Update 04/13/11 After returning these, I found cd sleeves by Maxwell that cost only a couple bucks more, but came in the exact type of quality my first two batches from Americopy came in. Their multi-colored, and although I would have preferred them to be all one color, at least I know the quality I'll be getting with Maxwell. Great purchase. I found my new CD sleeve "guy".
summary: Maxwell CD Sleeves!! Far better choice, for just a couple bucks more.

The Boston Acoustics LCAi220 has lots of features that initially make it attractive, but its serious flaws and oversights make it unusable for some of the key applications it is sold for - particularly connecting a local audio player, such as an iPod.On paper (electrons?!), the Boston Acoustics local control amplifier seemed to fit a need perfectly.  It's designed to let you share a pair of speakers between two sources- the first, an already amplified (speaker level) source, such as a whole house audio system or a stereo in another room driving B speakers/second zone; and- the second, a local line level preamplified source, such as a TV or an iPodWhen there's no local source, the LCAi220 essentially sits in standby, passing through the powered source to the speakers.  When the LCAi220 detects a local source, it switches to the local source, amplifies it, and drives the speakers.  So it would seem ideal for sources "like plasma TVs, PCs, MP3 players, gaming systems," as their marketing materials claim.But in fact it's really only able to handle video, and then only with some tweaking, due to some fatal design oversights.The key issue is that the auto-sensing feature which controls the switch to a local source isn't sensitive enough; and doesn't have a long enough delay built in.  So during quiet passages, or between songs, it switches the local source off; and then takes a while until it switches it back on.  That cuts off the beginning and end of songs.So in effect, you can't use the audio sensing feature on lots of applications, because it won't work predictably enough. And you can't adjust it to fit your situation.So that leaves a voltage trigger input, which can be used instead of the audio input sensing.  With video (or a serious audio system) it would be fairly easy to add a cable to one of the TV's outputs and run it to the trigger to keep the local source on; that would switch on and off with the TV.But for typical audio uses, where the LCAi220 is supposed to be most of the system, you won't have a 3-30V source you can easily run to the trigger.  So you'd have to jury-rig some kind of trigger to keep it switched to the local source, as well as some way to control that.It's not especially "installer friendly", as their website and the description above claims, because there's very little adjustment or flexibility to allow you to customize it to a particular installation.  They claim:  "Installer selectable delay and sensitivity adjustments." But these features must have been dropped, or be undocumented, since there seems to be no way to actually do either of these. That would fix the above problem, by the way.All of that's a shame, because on paper (before I tried to set it up), it looked very promising.- It's a very compact amplifier- It has some thoughtful features, such as a sub out for the local source (but see below)- The local source can be either line level or speaker level, as there are inputs for both.- It has fault detection and protection (shorts, overheating).If there's a way around the audio problem, other than rigging a voltage trigger, it's not documented.  No one at Boston Acoustics support will respond to calls and messages, so if the feature promised on the website is there, it's going to stay hidden it seems.If I'd known the audio sensing would be unusable and not adjustable, I'd have gone right to another product that used just a voltage trigger.There are several other problems or oddities that are problematic:- While the fact that there's a sub out for the local source is nice, the crossover points (30hz and 100hz) don't make much sense for the kind of speakers you're likely to use.  60hz and 120hz would work better with typical  bookshelf / full range speakers and with small satellite speakers, respectively.- Oddly, if you disconnect the power there's a too loud noise sent to the speakers.- Most importantly, it's underpowered.  The 10W into 8 ohms output isn't at all conservative, it seems, so you need to use lower ohm / higher sensitivity speakers to get enough out of the system.  (It delivers 20 watts at 4 ohms.)  So even if your setup lets you deal with the auto-switching issues, the LCAi220 doesn't have enough power to give you flexibility with speaker choices.The Boston Acoustics LCAi220 seems like a product that they decided to ship before they'd really finished the design, testing and implementation.
summary: Looked promising, but ultimately very disappointing

I bought this unit for three specific there reasons. One, because it supported dualband-N WiFi and two, because it had USB ports to directly connect a printer and an external hard drive for file sharing, and three because it had a built in router/firewall/Giga-switch.  THe router/switch works great with decent tuning capabilities on the firewall. The WiFi portion is great. You can setup simultaneous 2.4 and 5.2 Ghz spectrums supporting A/B/G/N. For example, my EVO 4G WiFi doesn't support N-band, so I setup a 2.4 G SSID with WPA/PSK for it while my laptop support full N-Band specs so I setup a 5.2GHz N-Band SSID with WPA-2/AES/PSK for it. Both work at the same time. The only limitation is that the N-Band is only 300mbps if the 2.4 band is in use. But heck, that's faster than my Internet provider so I'm not complaining.  The USB ports is where this device fails miserably.  Setting up a printer on one of the ports is cumbersome at best and really painful most of the time. I'm a computer professional (that means I get paid for working on and securing computers for 30 years) so I know my way around technology. If I'm not familiar with it, I at least know how to dig in and figure it out.  When you attach the printer to the USB port, it's not like a network printer. There is a special utility you have to run on every computer that you want to print to the USB port and then the drivers don't work half the time. I set it up, got it printing, then the next thing I printed spit out 20 pages of driver mish-mash ASCII characters. And this is regardless of OS - I set it up on my XP, Vista, and Win7 machines. I wound up aborting the attempt and just used the network functionality of the laser printer and hooked it up directly to the switch.  On to the attempt to setup an external harddrive. This is even worse. The protocol is FTP, not UNC file sharing, so you can't "map a drive" in windows like other shared drives. You can setup up DDNS so you can access your harddrive from the Internet, but so can everyone else on the Internet. And you have to do that if you want to setup an internal access path. At least I couldn't get it to work without it. After two hours of searching the 'Net for help I was able to get the device to show up in my windows explorer as a network resource (the FTP works fine, but you can't use it as an iTunes share via network resources), but I couldn't delete or add anything to the drive, even though I had admin rights and was logged in to the drive. I tried searching ASUS's knowledge base, but that is no use and their tech support is worthless. I sat on hold for hours and inally gave up. The documentation is terrible and the on-screen help is no better. I would have given this a 5-star rating if not for the USB ports.
